He also [fact-checked **Dwarkesh Patel**'s dramatic framing](/?date=2026-09-01&category=social#item-b9fe0ec47c36) and [launched a viral $1M AGI bet](/?date=2026-09-01&category=social#item-67bc2df3bc57) against **Elon Musk**.

- **François Chollet**, the benchmark's own creator, [disputed a claimed 100% **ARC-AGI-3** score](/?date=2026-09-01&category=social#item-80427c8f0e57), keeping benchmark integrity in focus.
- **Hugging Face** CEO **Delangue** shared ecosystem milestones: [10,000+ microduck preorders](/?date=2026-09-01&category=social#item-fb918ad1593e) and [4PB of weekly uploads](/?date=2026-09-01&category=social#item-f0f066cb2689).

Overall sentiment: anxious about agent autonomy, yet pushing back on hype, overclaiming, and overcautious guardrails alike.

In July, we reported three incidents...
items.content:
We’re sharing an update on our alignment and security efforts.

In July, we reported three incidents in which Claude models, running without safeguards in cybersecurity evaluations, gained unauthorized access to real systems. 

In a new post, we describe:

1. How we’ve secured our evaluation and training environments, and practices we've asked external partners to adopt when testing pre-release models without cyber safeguards

2. An update on our alignment assessment

3. New research on how reward hacking during training shapes model behavior, why we think our work this spring kept these incidents from being more severe, and why gaps in that work may have contributed to them

4. How we hardened our security practices earlier this year to prepare for Mythos-class models

Read more: https://t.co/E3Ea1Ds814

Solaris is a new kind of operating system that generates interactive interfaces frame by frame, in real time, with no code. Like it wouldn't download and install a 19...
items.content:
I keep rejected by Claude for the most benign things now

Like it wouldn't download and install a 1990s game from archive(dot)org because of copyright

The safety guardrails in a way make it more dangerous not less I think because after rejecting you it becomes kind of a pedantic child that will just reject whatever

If in that moment your server will go down and it feels it's related it could just reject fixing it

I'm confused how Anthropic is fumbling their lead so much with this stuff, I love to use Claude Code but they're kinda forcing me to move elsewhere to actually get my work done

Also the irony knowing that every single LLM is trained on billions of pages of copyrighted data

items.title:
This is a cool idea: a learning platform for agents.

Basically, this helps agents improve using the...
items.content:
This is a cool idea: a learning platform for agents.

Basically, this helps agents improve using their real production experience. In other words: agents learn from what they do and what happens because of it.

Some of the highlights:

• It extracts potential lessons from production traffic
• It validates those lessons using reinforcement learning
• It evaluates whether those behaviors improve the agents
• It uses those learnings to improve the agents

They report 36% fewer failed tasks and 57% lower token costs for agents working on tasks that they encountered before.

items.title: I'm excited to announce that Julia Brau Donnelly will be joining Sierra as our Chief Financial Offic...
items.content:
I'm excited to announce that Julia Brau Donnelly will be joining Sierra as our Chief Financial Officer.

Julia has seen companies from almost every side: as an investment banker, a private-equity investor, an operator at Wayfair, and as CFO of Pinterest. That range of experience and adaptability is so valuable in an industry that is changing at a pace none of us have seen before. Most of all, Julia embodies our culture: low ego, high agency, and excited to roll up her sleeves to get the work done. And there’s a lot of building to do. 

Just two and a half years since launch, Sierra has become the leading customer-facing conversational AI platform. The business is growing much faster than even our most optimistic predictions, hitting $100M in ARR in just seven quarters and $200M in nine quarters. We now work with over 40% of the Fortune 50, one in three of the leading banks, five out of 10 of the largest healthcare companies in the world, and 25% of the IBEX 35. With the shift from one-and-done service agents to revenue-aligned long-horizon agents, the opportunity for Sierra just got much, much bigger. 

Julia — welcome to Sierra! @claybavor and I are so excited to have you on the team.

There's a fascinating new startup using dogs to detect cancer in human breath

In a new trial, the d...
items.content:
There's a fascinating new startup using dogs to detect cancer in human breath

In a new trial, the dogs detected it over 90% of the time!

How it works:

Dognosis has patients breathe into a cotton surgical mask, which is then frozen and shipped to their farm in India.

There, a dog works a line of 10 samples. One beagle breezed past the first five, stopped at the sixth, moved away, came back, and circled it for several seconds.

To her, the whole thing is a game, and the reward is a treat.

But the dog is only half the system. Sensors track each dog's movement, body language, and brain activity.

A probabilistic model then combines signals from multiple dogs, weighted by each dog's historical accuracy, into a single score.

In a study of over 3,000 people, that system caught 90.8% of the real cancers, and correctly cleared 91.3% of the people who didn't have any.

The catch is that this was from a case-control study, where researchers already knew who had cancer (finding rare cases hidden in a healthy population is a harder problem).

BUT a larger trial is running now across 10 Indian hospitals.

If it holds up, we might use dogs to help detect cancer in the future

Codex/Claude Code c...
items.content:
Codex/Claude Code and Grok use two different approaches to control the browser.

Codex/Claude Code controls it from the inside (via an extension), while Grok controls it from the outside (via the OS API).

I'm not comfortable with Grok. Not only does it expose your computer to higher risks, but it's also just inconvenient: when Grok is working with the browser, you cannot use your computer at all because of the interference between what you do and what Grok is doing. It's especially weird when both of you use the clipboard at the same time.

items.title:
AI and the Memory Wall!

Researchers from UC Berkeley, ICSI + LBNL found that over the past 20 years...
items.content:
AI and the Memory Wall!

Researchers from UC Berkeley, ICSI + LBNL found that over the past 20 years, peak compute performance increased about 3× every two years, while DRAM bandwidth increased only about 1.6× and interconnect bandwidth about 1.5×.

Berkeley AI paper’s 20-year projection:

Compute = 60,000× increase
DRAM Bandwidth = 100× increase
Interconnect Bandwidth = 30× increase

Compute has therefore scaled about 600× faster than DRAM bandwidth over the same period.

To keep pace with AI compute scaling, memory bandwidth would need to grow roughly 3× every two years, not the historical 1.6×.

For a 70B LLM generating 100 tokens/sec, even weight streaming alone can require several TB/s of effective HBM bandwidth, illustrating why HBM has become critical for modern AI systems.

My guess is that we'll have AI that is smarter than any one human probably around the end of next year [2025]”

Elon today: same thing, just silently moved back the prediction by two years, this time to end of 2027.

No accountability, and he will just keep doing this indefinitely.

items.content:
Most enterprises treat modernization like a renovation: start date, end date, budget line. 

In the AI era that mindset is a liability. 

AI coding agents write code faster. 

They don't make it easier to maintain. 

Tech debt piles up faster than teams can clear it.

items.title: Video is a richer training signal than still images because it contains motion and temporal order, b...
items.content:
Video is a richer training signal than still images because it contains motion and temporal order, but learning useful representations from unlabeled video has usually required much more computation and extra machinery to stop “representation collapse,” where a network maps every input to essentially the same output.

This paper from @amilabs, @BrownUniversity, @DKTK_, @DKFZ, @Mila_Quebec, @nyuniversity, and @UMontreal explores whether that complexity is actually necessary. 

LeVJEPA trains a single video transformer by making representations of different views of the same clip agree, while a statistical regularizer called SIGReg keeps the learned representations spread out in a well-defined distribution, preventing collapse without a second encoder, a predictor network, or special gradient blocking.

The practical consequence is substantial: the model can discard 95% of video tokens during training, reducing computation while improving some downstream accuracy, and it matches or exceeds V-JEPA 2 with roughly 5.6–20.8× less pretraining compute; under equal compute it is substantially stronger on ImageNet and Kinetics-400.

It also shows that attention can be made causal across time—each frame is represented using only that frame and earlier ones—without a measurable accuracy loss, which matters for streaming systems and models that must predict what happens next.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/kybwAgrEBN

Ran rebuilt his family's shared birthday fund as a Claude-built web app, with five contributors, a fixed amount per birthday, and an exemption rule for whoever's celebrating.

When a closed browser tab wiped the real family data, he turned the failure into features like CSV backups, a backup-reminder alert, and a 46-test suite Claude ran on its own work.

items.title: Giga G-Type Main Sequence Star Sun Life: When the Sun Dies a Giant Crystal Will Take Its Place - A d...
items.content:
Giga G-Type Main Sequence Star Sun Life: When the Sun Dies a Giant Crystal Will Take Its Place - A diamond tombstone the size of our planet.  @NASA 

It's Been a Good Ride

An argument for why human civilization has to colonize galaxies

It's been a good ride, but the Sun is dying! It has been burning for 5 Giga years = 5 Billion years.

Not a metaphorical death. A calculable death, printed in the physics of a G-type main-sequence star that has been converting hydrogen into helium and time for roughly 5 billion years and will keep doing so for about five billion more (National Aeronautics and Space Administration [NASA], n.d.-a). We are nearly 5 billion years into a stellar lifetime, of big bang and the sun is dying.  Popular Mechanics' technology desk put the sun’s death in a headline that reads like a line of description of a phase transition: When the Sun Dies, a Giant Crystal Will Take Its Place (Popular Mechanics, 2019). Our star will bloat, shed its envelope, collapse to an Earth-sized cinder, and then slowly, over billions of years — freeze solid into a crystallized sphere of carbon and oxygen. A diamond tombstone the size of a planet.

The clock we actually have is not five billion years

The five billion year number is the Sun's clock, not ours. Our clock on earth is much shorter, because a star does not need to die to kill a biosphere, it only needs to get brighter. The Sun's luminosity climbs roughly one percent every 110 million years, and modeling of Earth's future carbon-climate system puts the collapse of the plant biosphere somewhere in the range of 1.3 to 1.9 billion years from now, with atmospheric oxygen following the vegetation down (Popular Mechanics, 2026). Long before the phase of red giant, long before the crystal, Earth becomes a hot, deoxygenated rock with microbes in the margins.

So the real deadline for human civilization is not five billion. It is on the order of a billion — and the deadline for a technological civilization of human race, that needs stable agriculture and a breathable atmosphere and something like a climate, is shorter still. Everything after that requires us to be somewhere else outside solar system. Starts with Moon, Mars and then to another galaxy.

"Somewhere else in chaos" is not guaranteed to be gentle. We have now watched a star eat one of its own planets in real time: Astronomers caught the flash of a Jupiter-scale world spiraling into its host and being consumed (NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory [JPL], 2023; Popular Mechanics, n.d.-a). The Sun's own expansion is expected to devour its inner children — Mercury, Venus, and very likely Earth (Popular Mechanics, n.d.-b; European Space Agency [ESA], n.d.). This is the ordinary death of an ordinary star, repeated across the galaxy several hundred billion times (Scientific American, n.d.). 

We are the aliens

Here is the harder claim, and that changes the moral weight of everything above.

The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. The arrow of time runs one way. Stars of the Sun's mass burn for roughly ten billion years and then stop. Which means the great majority of Sun-like stars formed in the universe's first few billion years — during the peak of cosmic star formation — have already finished. Their main sequences ended. Their planets were scorched, swallowed, or stripped and rained back down onto the white dwarf remnant (https://t.co/26xSX4YxTg, n.d.). Whatever chemistry, whatever biology, whatever civilizations those systems produced had their billion-year windows and closed them, long before the Earth had continents in place.

Heavier stars are worse: an O- or B-type giant burns through its fuel in a few million years, a span that on Earth would not have gotten us past the first fish. There is no time there to build anything.

The inference is uncomfortable and, I think, correct: we may not be latecomers to a crowded galaxy. We may be one of the first crews on shift. May be because we are the chosen by the God, because the timing window for a technological species is narrow, the stars that support it are mortal, and the universe has not been running long enough to have had many overlapping turns. If nobody is broadcasting, the most economical explanation is not that they are hiding. It is that the stars before us are already dead, and the stars after us have not yet begun.

Read honestly, that is an inference, not a proof — absence of a signal is weak evidence, and the sampling is thin, but it is the reading most consistent with stellar physics and with the silence and if it is right, then we are the aliens. We are the strange, improbable, carbon-based visitors who show up somewhere and change what that place is in the infinite space of the universe. The only question is whether we ever actually show up anywhere.

This is not an argument that we are first in the universe. We are somewhere in the middle of the universe's habitable era, and the honest position is that if advanced civilizations exist, they must be 7 billion years away from us, but knowing and reaching are different problems. A civilization seven billion light-years away is not seven billion years in the past — they exist now, and what we see of them is simply reminiscent memory of light. The difficulty is not distance. It is that space is expanding at an accelerating pace, and accelerating beyond a certain distance the gap grows faster than anything can cross it at the speed of light. Not a hard journey. Those civilizations and ours are causally severed, permanently, in both directions. The reachable universe is shrinking, and it will keep shrinking. Whoever else is out there, most of them are already unreachable depending if their stars still live today and so are we, to them. Not because nobody exists in the space, but because the geometry forbids it. Laws of Physics forbid it. Whatever happens to Earth is ours to solve.

The long lived real estate is orange and red

If the argument stopped at "everything dies tonight, everybody dies tonight," it would be an argument for despair. It isn't, because the sky is not uniformly mortal.

Sun-like stars are the short-lease properties. The durable stars are smaller and cooler. K-type orange dwarfs — often called Goldilocks stars — burn for something like 15 to 44 billion years, hot enough for a comfortable habitable zone, calm enough to spare a planet the flare bombardment that plagues the smallest stars. Below them, M-type red dwarfs run for hundreds of billions to trillions of years, outlasting not just the Sun but the entire era of Sun-like star formation. They are also the most common stars in the galaxy by a wide margin.

That is the destination. Not because those systems are hospitable today, but because they are the only addresses with a lease long enough to matter. A civilization that gets to a stable K-dwarf system has not bought a billion years. It has bought tens of billions.

Moon, then Mars, then the rest

None of which is reachable without the complicated step.

The Moon is the proving ground: three days out and a place to learn closed loop life support, radiation shielding, regolith construction, and in-situ resource extraction under conditions where a failure is survivable and a rescue is conceivable. Nobody learns to keep humans alive off-world by starting at the hard journey.

Mars is the first genuine independent, self-sustaining node of the species, far enough away that no single asteroid, no single pathogen, no single war takes both.

Everything after that — Europa, Titan, free-flying habitats, and eventually the K- and M-dwarf systems — is the long project, measured in centuries of engineering and millennia of transit. It cannot begin in the century before just before the deadline. It has to begin while things are still easy.

The Giant crystal

The Sun will not become a black hole; it is far too light (NASA, n.d.-b). It will become a crystal from G-Main sequence star. In about ten billion years, our star will be a cold, dense, translucent sphere roughly the size of Earth, glittering silently in a galaxy that has moved on.

That is a beautiful ending, and it is coming whether or not anyone is around to describe it. The only variable we control is whether anyone remains who remembers what the Sun looked like from the ground — someone standing under an orange dwarf, tens of billions of years from now, telling the story of a small blue planet and a star that turned to diamond.

It's been a good ride. Let's make sure it isn't the whole trip.

items.title: P.S. The @NASA ADC (Astronomical Data Center) had 3 target audiences, with the primary and overarchi...
items.content:
P.S. The @NASA ADC (Astronomical Data Center) had 3 target audiences, with the primary and overarching audience being the world’s research scientists (mainly astronomers).

The other 2 audience groups that the web portal and data curation activities were designed to accommodate were: the general public and educators (including their students). 

Nancy Roman was always a strong advocate and contributor to these additions and enhancements of ADC’s web data portal, data products, and educational content. And she lived that passion outside of work with visits to schools and science clubs in the DC-MD-VA capital region. 

I remember attending at least one of those meetings with her, but the memory of it is now too faded for me to remember any details. It might have involved a knitting circle, with knitted space scapes being the objective.😎 Nancy was nearly 80 years old at that time. Though I was much younger, I may be totally misremembering the event. 

Disclaimer: the 2 attached scarf images were created by Grok AI today.

items.title: “The field of machine learning is concerned with the question of how to construct computer programs ...
items.content:
“The field of machine learning is concerned with the question of how to construct computer programs that automatically improve with experience.”
— from the Preface of “Machine Learning” by Tom Mitchell — download PDF of this classic ML book here: https://t.co/l2B7UG6trC

In 1998, when I discovered this book and read that first sentence, I paused, reread it, and pondered “what sort of mathematics is this?”

I had many years of advanced math in physics undergrad and astrophysics grad school, but this was a totally new perspective for me. And it redirected the entire trajectory of my career.

One of the early products of my career redirection was this website that I created and maintained at @NASAGoddard for several years: "Data Mining Resources for Space Science" (shut down in 2002; now preserved on the Internet Archive Wayback Machine): https://t.co/dAXGqZFHrr

items.title:
You've been Informed! 

If Springer or Springer Nature officially labels a scholarly book OPEN ACCES...
items.content:
You've been Informed! 

If Springer or Springer Nature officially labels a scholarly book OPEN ACCESS, then the eBook is FREE to read and download. That is exactly what Open Access means.

You do NOT have to purchase the eBook or pay for any weekly/monthly subscription.

Springer Nature explicitly states that its Open Access books are freely available online and says:

“Download any of our OA books for free.”

Critical Thinking --> On Springer Nature Link, Open Access books are even clearer: the page typically states “You have full access to this open access Book” and provides direct:

Download book PDF
Download book EPUB
No paid subscription is required.

If a Springer download workflow ever asks you to sign in or create an account, do not confuse an account/login step with a paywall. It's just for you to create credentials with Springer. The defining issue is whether the scholarly digital edition is officially designated OPEN ACCESS.

Paperback/Hardcover ≠ Open Access eBook.

The physical edition may still carry a normal retail price. Open Access applies to the scholarly digital edition, unless the publisher explicitly states otherwise.

So seeing a $50, $80 or $150 price for the printed book does NOT mean the Open Access eBook costs money.

OPEN ACCESS = FREE DIGITAL ACCESS.

Quantum Technologies — Free Springer Nature Open Access eBook!

Julian Jang,  Philippe Caroff, et al.’s Springer 2026 book is a 239-page Open Access reference covering the rapidly evolving intersection of Quantum Computing, Machine Learning, AI Supercomputing + Cybersecurity.

• Quantum Computing
• Quantum Machine Learning
• Quantum Optimization
• Quantum Annealing
• AI Supercomputing for Quantum Computing
• Superconducting Qubits
• Trapped-Ion Quantum Computers
• Neutral-Atom Quantum Computing
• Semiconductor Spin Qubits
• Quantum Error Control + Mitigation
• Quantum Communication
• Quantum Key Distribution
• Post-Quantum Cryptography
• Quantum Random Number Generation
• Quantum Threats + Readiness

Across 22 chapters, the book brings together research and insights from 40+ experts worldwide, spanning both the computational foundations of quantum systems and their emerging implications for AI, optimization, HPC, cryptography, next-generation computing.

Springer Nature explicitly marks the entire book Open Access — free and unlimited access, with the complete PDF + EPUB available to download.

items.summary_html: Kirk Borne shares a personal tribute to Dr. Nancy Roman, NASA's first Chief Astronomer, describing his years as contract manager overseeing her data curation work at Goddard's Astronomy Data Center. Historical science remembrance, only loosely adjacent to AI via data curation.
items.content_html:
After retiring from her leadership role as @NASA’s Chief Astronomer, Dr. Nancy Roman continued working many more years as a contractor scientist in @NASAGoddard’s ADC (Astronomy Data Center). For ~8 of those years, I was the contract manager overseeing the data curation activities of the ADC and ADF (Astrophysics Data Facility) contractor staff, including Nancy. She was a treasure to us as she continued significant contributions to the work of astronomical research scientists worldwide through her expertise in curating large numbers of astronomical data catalogs from scientists, universities, observatories, and other organizations around the world.

Flashback via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine: https://t.co/bSx5g3uNKG

@NASARoman

items.title: I'm not religious, but even I know that for a religious person, only their religion is the true one ...
items.content:
I'm not religious, but even I know that for a religious person, only their religion is the true one leading to paradise, while all other people who aren't of their religion, atheists, or agnostics will go to hell for the simple reason of not doing the daily practices that the religion requires or not wearing the magical clothes required by the only true God.

If it weren't the case, then religion wouldn't be considered a protected property similar to skin color or gender. The possibility of freely choosing and deliberately switching between religions would disqualify it as such a property to be protected.

So, when you have a single majority religion in some country, people automatically assume that they all go to the same and only paradise unless someone among them deliberately commits some act that would bar their access to paradise.

On the other hand, when you have a plurality of religions in a country, each small group sharing a religion only considers the members of their group saved, while the majority of their co-citizens will go to hell, including neighbors, colleagues, friends, and family members, thus not deserving to be cared about as much as their religious co-fellows with whom they will be sharing eternity in paradise.

Now live with this.

items.content_html:
@onejasonknight In Quebec, condominiums and apartment buildings already ban putting flags in the windows (on the inside of the apartment).

Also, homeowners must abide by the city's architectural code, so, for example, you cannot paint your house in the color of your choice.

So, the legal basis is already there. Anytime they could add a "no-flag" clause into the city's architectural code, and everyone would be fined for not complying.
